newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - France offers little to tempt buyers.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - France offers little to tempt buyers.

text.p: International bond investors, already avoiding the French debt market, will find little value from the European Union's decision to allow a controversial plan to reduce France's budget deficit, analysts said on Thursday.

"The structural problems in France and the government's seeming inability to do anything about them will continue to drive away overseas interest," said Gwyn Hacche, international economist at HSBC-James Capel in London.
"The Telecom issue is only short term, and won't change anything," he said.

The EU said on Thursday it would allow the French government to include a transfer from France Telecom funds to reduce its 1997 budget deficit in order to meet the Maastricht criteria for European Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).
Earlier in the week, a German central banker had criticised the plan as creative accounting, and warned that it jeopardised the drive towards the single currency.
Analysts said that overseas investors take a wary view of French debt at a time when unemployment is at a record high and the economy is stagnant.
"The Bank of France hasn't got much leeway to lower interest rates and today's figures will make it difficult politically for taxes to be increased," said Hacche.
Earlier, figures from France's labour ministry showed the September unemployment rate rose to a record 12.6 percent from 12.5 percent in August.

An opinion poll released on Tuesday said 96 percent of French voters felt anxious about the economic and social situation. Prime Minister Alain Juppe has this week also faced calls for a cabinet reshuffle, early elections or a referendum.

"It's hard to say what the upside is for French bonds," said Steve Englander, international economist at Smith Barney in Paris. "I wouldn't advise buying French bonds at two years and out unless the spread over Germany is about 30 basis points -- ten points isn't enough," he said.

The spread of two-year French bonds over comparable German debt was at 21 basis points by 1230 GMT, the three-year spread was at 12 basis points. There was, however, some value to be had at the very short end, as analysts said the Bank of France could trim the intervention rate a further, after a five basis point cut on Thursday which took the rate to 3.20 percent.
Englander said most French bonds would remain caught in a range, as overseas investors have already quit the market, and domestic investors would sit tight.

But some analysts said domestic investors, particularly life insurance companies, would start to move up the curve in search of value. They added that paper which is potentially post-EMU would be less volatile, they said.
"Pre-1999 paper could be subjected to an attack on mark/Paris or to a Bank of France rate hike," said Steve Major, Paris-based head of bond research at Credit Lyonnais.
"The 1999 onwards paper will be under the European Central Bank so it will effectively trade like the euro."

Major said it was inconsistent for investors to buy French debt dated before 1999 if they viewed EMU as a likely event. He said some investors were selling French paper in 1998 and switching into 1999.

Englander said investors would also look in vain for currency movements to add spice to French bonds. He said the maximum move for the mark/Paris rate was to 3.3500. It stood at 3.3744/54 by 1300 GMT.
"Forget French bonds and playing on the exchange rate," said Englander. "If you want to go into France, take a look at equities."
